item.title: No-Bake Pistachio & Vanilla Cheesecake
item.description:
This is a work in progress, based off a poorly written recipe on Instagram.

In the video, it looks like they use pistachio paste as a topping instead of pistachio cream, but the pistachio cream (which I used) was very tasty. Pistachio paste would be more savoury and is worth experimenting with (the translation and comments disagree on whether the video uses paste or cream). The pistachio layer also looks larger than what their recipe describes. I followed the written recipe, but I suspect using 3 tbsp of each component in the crunch layer would give a better result.

Some of the ingredients here can be hard to find outside of an Italian grocery store, but they can be bought online, and are easy enough to make yourself:

  • Pistachio praline paste: you can use store-bought, but it's hard to find. Not pistachio paste; pistachio paste is not a substitute.
  • Pistachio cream: you can use store-bought. Not pistachio paste, which is just pure pistachio butter; this is pistachio paste + white chocolate and milk. You could sub pistachio paste for a more savoury taste.
  • Feuilletine: better to use store-bought crêpes dentelles than try to make this. Unless you have an amazing non-stick crêpe pan, don't make these, just buy them. If you can't find them, replace them with any other butter cookie.
  • Cookie base: use Biscoff cookies.

Pistachio cream

Ingredients

  • 140g shelled pistachios, skins off, unsalted
  • 1/2 tsp salt
  • 1 tbsp sugar
  • 180ml whole milk
  • 25g unsalted butter
  • 100g white chocolate

Method

Make the paste: Blitz the pistachios in the food processor until coarse. Add the salt, sugar, and 2 tbsp of the milk. Blend for around 5 minutes until the pistachios turn into a smooth pistachio paste, scraping down the sides every minute or so. Be patient: to begin with, it will resemble breadcrumbs, but eventually it will turn into a paste. If after 5 minutes it is struggling, add a bit more milk.

Melt the chocolate: Meanwhile, melt the butter and white chocolate with the rest of the milk over low heat.

Blend: Add the white chocolate mixture to the food processor and blend until very smooth. If you want it super smooth, transfer to a blender.

Store: Store in an airtight container and chill until needed.

Notes:

  • You want the pistachio cream as smooth as you can get it for a nice topping on the cake.
  • Doing the whole thing in a blender requires a higher volume of nuts, so double the recipe if you don't want to wash two machines. Pistachio cream can be frozen.
  • If the pistachios you buy have skins on, you can blanch them in boiling water, then rub them in a tea towel to remove the skins.

Pistachio praline paste

Ingredients

  • 150g shelled, unsalted pistachios
  • 120g white sugar
  • Pinch of salt

Method

Roast the pistachios: Preheat the oven to 350°F. Spread the pistachios evenly in one layer on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper, with enough space between them; try not to crowd them. Bake for 6–8 minutes in the middle of the oven, until fragrant and lightly browned.

Get ready: Set out a piece of parchment paper on a heat-proof surface or baking sheet.

Make a dry caramel: Use a heavy-bottomed 3-quart pot. Pour in the sugar, spreading it evenly so you get one thin layer. Place over medium heat and allow the sugar to begin to melt without stirring. Once you see melted, caramelized areas, gently push the undissolved sugar crystals towards the melted sugar with a heatproof spatula, avoiding the sides of the pot. Lower the heat to avoid burning.

Add the nuts: When the caramel turns amber and you see your first wisp of smoke, remove from the heat and add a pinch of salt. Caramelizing will take about 15 minutes on low heat. Immediately add the roasted pistachios, stir, then pour onto your prepared parchment. Cool at room temperature until hard.

Mix the paste: Break the caramel into small pieces and place in the food processor bowl with the pistachios and salt. Process, occasionally scraping the bowl, until the praline paste becomes slightly runny and shiny. This will take a while, about 15 minutes. If your food processor gets hot at any point, stop mixing and let it rest for 5 minutes. If your food processor isn't powerful enough, or the pistachios were a bit dry, you might need to add a little neutral vegetable oil to loosen the paste.

Store: Store in an airtight container and chill until needed.

Pistachio & vanilla cheesecake

Ingredients

Base

  • 200g Biscoff cookies (speculoos)
  • 90g butter, melted

Pistachio layer

  • 2 tbsp pistachio cream
  • 2 tbsp pistachio praline paste
  • 2 tbsp crêpes dentelles

Cheesecake layer

  • 300g cream cheese, room temperature
  • 1 tbsp pistachio cream
  • 100g sugar
  • 1 vanilla bean
  • Pinch of salt
  • 1/4 tsp cream of tartar
  • 150g cold whipping cream

Topping

  • 1/2 cup pistachio cream

Method

This recipe is for an 8" cake; for a 9" cake, increase the recipe by 130%.

Make the base: Use an 8" springform cake pan. Blitz the Biscoff cookies in a food processor until a fine crumb forms, then add the melted butter. Spread in your cake pan, creating a uniform base and sides 1.5" tall. Put in the fridge to firm up while you work on the rest.

Make the pistachio layer: Mix the pistachio cream, pistachio praline paste, and crumbled-up crêpes dentelles. It will be a thick layer with crunchy bits. Use an offset spatula to spread this as a thin layer on top of the cookie base. Return to the fridge.

Make the cheesecake layer: To a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, add the cream cheese, sugar, salt, cream of tartar, and the scraped-out seeds of the vanilla bean. Beat on medium speed until smooth. Switch to the whisk attachment, add the whipping cream, and beat until stiff peaks form. Pour into the cookie base, using an offset spatula to smooth the top. Return to the fridge for 4 hours.

Add the pistachio cream topping: Warm up the pistachio cream until it is smooth and spreadable, but not hot. Pour over the cream cheese layer and return to the fridge until firm.

Serve: Serve cold, right from the fridge. It would be great with coffee.

Notes

  • The first time I made this, I whipped the whipping cream separately and did not get it to stiff peaks, so the cheesecake was quite runny but very delicious. I adjusted here based on the Serious Eats steps for a no-bake cheesecake, and I also added cream of tartar as a stabilizer.
  • You could also prepare this as a soft mousse inside parfait cups for individual servings, which can help if the filling is runny.
  • I suspect you could increase the pistachio layer to 3 tbsp of each component for a better crunch layer.
  • My friends I shared this with said it would be amazing frozen as an ice cream cake.

item.title: Oyster mushroom, sausage, fennel, and honey pasta
item.description:
Ingredients

  • 1/2 lb oyster mushrooms (or whatever kind you like) – broken into pieces
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 2 cloves of garlic, thinly sliced
  • 1lb Italian sausage, removed from the casing
  • 1 tbsp fennel seeds
  • 2 tbsp tomato paste
  • 2 tbsp honey
  • 1 tsp (or more) chili flakes
  • 1/2 cup grated parmesan
  • 1lb dried pasta, a fun shape with nooks and crannies
  • 1 cup pasta water
  • Salt and pepper

Note:

For oyster mushrooms, break the smaller mushrooms directly off, but for the larger mushrooms tear them into smaller pieces. If using another mushroom, but into 1-2” pieces (for example, sliced cremini mushrooms can be left just like that).

Method

Set a large pan on medium-high heat. Add the oil and butter. When the butter foams, add the mushrooms. Ignore the mushrooms for 5–7 minutes until they get a good sear on one side, then stir them, lightly salt them, and cook another 5–7 minutes until brown.

Add the sliced garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant, don’t burn the garlic.

Add the sausage and break it up with a spoon, cooking it until it gets a nice level of brownness.

Add the fennel seeds and black pepper, and stir to coat in the fat, about 30 seconds.

Add the tomato paste and cook for 1–2 minutes.

Add the honey and chilli flakes to taste.

Remove from the heat and add half the parmesan. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

Boil your pasta per their cooking directions in heavily salted water. Reserve 1 cup of pasta water. Drain the pasta. Add the pasta to your pan with the sausage (or add everything to very large bowl). Add pasta water, stirring, until a smooth sauce forms. The pasta water and the cooking fat will continue emulsifying as you stir, so keep adding pasta water and stirring until you get a glossy sauce.

Top with the remaining parmesan and serve, ideally with a sharp salad.

item.title: Travel Canada
item.description:
Canadians spend 1% of our GDP on travel to the US

Collectively, Canadians $20.5 billion on travel to the US annually, supporting 110,000 US jobs – equivalent to 1% of Canada’s GDP.

Our Prime Minster, Justin Trudeau, shared this week that Donald Trump is serious about trying to annex Canada. This will likely be a functional impossibility with how the Canadian constitution works, and how a physical invasion would be nearly impossible from a physical logistics, global politics, and American politics perspective.

But here we are, talking it about. So what can we do?

We can change how we spend our money.

Canadians are mad, not sorry

While the tariffs may be off, Canadians are very mad, and it’s America’s turn to say sorry. I don’t think words can articulate how deep the rage runs within Canadians right now. The rage that our closest friend, ally, and neighbour would not only try to destroy our economy with tariffs, but repeatedly diminish the leader of our country and our sovereignty as an independent nation.

The rage has to go somewhere, so I wanted to give you my pitch for travelling within Canada this year, and keeping those tourism dollars in the Canadian economy.

If you want to hit America where it hurts, the economy, here is my advice:

  • Cancel your vacations to the US (yes. this includes Hawaii)
  • Spend your money on vacations in Canada
  • If you work in marketing for a Canadian company, move your annual conference to Canada – make Americans come spend money here
  • Stop shopping in the US: it’s the #1 tourist activity for Canadians visiting the US

From Far and Wide, Oh Canada

I’ve spent much of my life exploring other countries – international travel sounds very glamorous – but there’s so much to see here at home. Our country is big, beautiful, and diverse.

Last September, I did something I’ve always wanted to do: I drove across Canada in an electric pick-up truck! (A Rivian R1T). It took me 5 days to drive across Ontario: Canada is gigantic, it is over 5,000km across.

Here was my route:

  • Kitchener, Ontario (near Toronto)
  • Bruce Peninsula National Park, Ontario
  • Lake Superior Provincial Park, Ontario
  • Rainbow Falls Provincial Park, Ontario
  • Rushing River Provincial Park, Ontario
  • Winnipeg, Manitoba
  • Riding Mountain National Park, Manitoba
  • Regina and Moosejaw, Saskatchewan
  • Grasslands National Park, Saskatchewan
  • Drumheller, Alberta
  • Banff National Park, Alberta
  • Kelowna, British Columbia
  • Lake Okanagan South Provincial Park, British Columbia
  • Nanaimo, British Columbia
  • Victoria, British Columbia

I then drove through the US National Parks on the way back, but we’ll pretend that never happened. When I got back to Ontario, I returned through cities:

  • Kitchener, Ontario
  • Ottawa, Ontario
  • Montreal, Quebec
  • Quebec City, Quebec
  • Fredericton, New Brunswick
  • Halifax, Nova Scotia
  • Annapolis Valley, Nova Scotia

While many people think of Canadian travel as the big cities (Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa) or the big parks on the West coast (Banff, Whistler), there is so much more to see.

My favourite places were the unexpected ones in rural areas – Rainbow Falls, Riding Mountain, and Grasslands were my favourite parks. Drumheller was a crazy dinosaur town filled with dinosaur statues and hoo-doos. Vancouver Island is just stunning and there is no place like it.

Montreal is my favourite city in Canada. Fredericton is a beautiful historic city, and Halifax is a much bigger metropolitan city than you expect.

I’m going to discuss the provinces east-to-west across the country, as the Maritimes are often forgotten for Canadian travel, yet are some of the most beautiful places in the entire world. This is not a complete list or a set of recommendations.

Please share your favourite places in Canada in the comments!

Newfoundland and Labrador

I went to Newfoundland in highschool for a leadership program. We hiked Mount Gros Morne, kayaked beside whales, and went to St. John’s to see icebergs floating by in the ocean. I don’t have photos of this, it was 21 years ago, but I remember it so vividly for how beautiful it was. St. John’s has George St., which is a giant pub crawl. And of course, Screech.

My friend Larysa recently took her family to Newfoundland and says: Gros Morne National Park: western brook pond tour. Canadian fjords. Amazing hiking. Twillinggate for whale watching. Icebergs depending on time of year. Cool little museum. Bonavista lighthouse, puffins, and maybe my fav hike of the east coast was the Skerwink Trail. St Johns for all the music and fun. Eat at the Noon & Canery and Gypsy Tea room

And if you’re bougie, there is always Fogo Island.

*Photo credit: Larysa Wood*

*Photo credit: Larysa Wood*

*Photo credit: Larysa Wood*

*Photo credit: Larysa Wood*

Prince Edward Island (PEI)

I haven’t been to PEI, it’s a goal of mine this summer. Most people know of PEI from Anne of Green Gables, and it’s iconic red sand beaches. My friend Michelle recently took her family there and raved about it. They stayed at BlackBush Beach Resort and raved about The Table Culinary Studio.

My friend Kayleen says: In the winter months be prepared to stay on Charlottetown as most attractions are for the summer, but there is so much to enjoy in town. there is the Gahan House (brewery and restaurant, you can see the original brewery in the basement), Anne of Green Gables, and you can walk the main roads to the Brighton lighthouse In the Summer, rent a car and drive the whole island or to New Brunswick across the massive bridge. Try Cavendish and see the red soil.

My friend Sybil says: “I go in August, I just spend my entire time on the beach. When the tide goes out and the tiny water level is a mirror scape.”

*Photo credit: Sybil O’Connor*

Nova Scotia

I recently moved to Nova Scotia, falling in love with how beautiful the landscape is and how kind the people are. I’ve been so struck with how wrong my assumptions about Nova Scotia have been. I now living in the Annapolis Valley region, 45 minutes from Halifax, and I’ve never been surrounded by better people, food, farming, views, activities, wineries, and more.

I live in Windsor, Nova Scotia – a town with 3,000 people and I have more fun here than I did in a city of 750,000 people. Last night I went to a sold out drag bingo show in a town of 3,000 people. 400 people came!** It’s incredibly welcoming and inclusive here.

The bakery here in Windsor, Bedard, challenges the best bakeries I’ve been to in Montreal for quality. (Arch & Po in Annapolis Royal is also excellent).

*Cape Forchu in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia*

*Lunenburg, a UNESCO World Heritage site*

*Historic Annapolis Royal*

I’m going to do a full pitch for Nova Scotia soon. The more I learn the more amazed I am at how much there is to see and do here, and I believe this to be true for all of Atlantic Canada.

But for your online research, here are some places to look up:

  • Halifax is the main city, with a ton of great food and entertainment options. Halifax has everything any big city has to offer, plus the ocean.
  • South Shore is the main tourist attraction: Peggy’s Cove, Mahone Bay, and Lunenburg
  • Just west of Halifax is some of the best surfing in Canada at Cow Bay
  • The Annapolis Valley (“The Valley”) is the most beautiful area to me: rolling hills, forests, ocean, farm fields, and small towns bursting with personality. There are over 20 wineries (that make excellent white wine), beer and cider breweries, farm-to-table restaurants like Bessie North House and Le Caveau, and tons of entertainment options. A few weeks ago I went to Salt Air Nordic Spa in Baxter’s Harbour and it’s the best Nordic spa I have ever been to – anywhere. Everywhere you look you have views of the ocean.
  • Cape Breton Island is the large, Eastern half of Nova Scotia. I haven’t been there yet, but it is world famous for the Cabot Trail, which my friends drove last year and said was absolutely stunning – rolling cliffs of trees in beautiful Fall colours. My hope is to visit this year.
  • Sable Island is a remote National Park in the Atlantic Ocean with stunning views and nature

*The view from an Airbnb I stayed at last Spring in Chester, on the South Shore of Nova Scotia.*

*Lunenburg being cute*

*A small portion of The Annapolis Valley as viewed from The Lookoff*

*A local art show in Bear River, Nova Scotia. There is a huge art culture here.*

New Brunswick

I haven’t spent much time in New Brunswick yet, only driven through it.

From my friend Kayleen: Saint John New Brunswick has an amazing market for veggies, seafood, and the occasional souvenir. St Andrews by the Bay is a quaint welcoming town on the Bay with a beautiful view and the Algonquin is a well known landmark as a vintage hotel/good course. Rothesay is beautiful. Walking along the road but be ready for some hills. Try out Pomodori Pizza Rothesay one of the best pizzas I've had. We ate there twice! Shadow lawn in is also a nice B&B.

From my friend KJ: I would recommend looking at Saint Andrews by the Sea. They have a lot of historic monuments, that are pretty cool to look at. I would also look into Fort Lewisburg, they did a restoration project in the early 2000s. Obviously, the valley. When I travel, I am big history, buff, so I like to connect to the historical side of things.

New Brunswick has three main centres: St. John, Fredericton, and Moncton, all within close driving distance of each other.

*Photo credit: Kayleen Hamelin*

*Photo credit: Kayleen Hamelin*

Québec

If you want to feel like you’ve gone to Europe, go to Quebec. Montreal and Quebec City are extraordinarily magical places. In general, you can get by with English in Montreal, but brush up on your French for Quebec City.

There are many beautiful small towns, like Saint-Jean-Port-Joli. You can go skiing in Tremblant. You can spend the summer in the amazing Quebec and Canadian National Parks, such as La Maurice and Gaspésie. There are hidden gems like The Magdalen Islands.

Quebec is geographically huge and culturally fantastic and worth exploring.

Here is a guide I previously wrote about Montreal (and a bit of Toronto, Ontario):

*Want to feel like you’re in Europe? Head to Montreal*

# Ontario

I spent 38 years of my life in Ontario. Ontario has so much stuff. It’s gigantic. Take your pick.

  • Head to Toronto for New York vibes
  • Prince Edward County or Niagara on the Lake for Napa vibes (Restaurant Pearl Morissette and RPM Bakehouse are world-class)
  • Niagara Falls for Vegas vibes
  • Ottawa for Washington, DC vibes
  • Any of the National or Provincial parks, from Alongquin for back-country camping to The Pinery for beaches to Bruce Peninsula for clear blue waters near historic Tobermory
  • Any of the beach towns along Lake Huron and Georgian Bay
  • Northern Ontario – once you pass Sault St Marie and into Thunder Bay – is unlike any other part of Canada. It’s this rugged, mountainous area that is so incredibly beautiful. I stayed in an off-grid cabin in Thunder Bay, near Sleeping Giant Provincial Park a couple of years ago.

Here is a guide I previously wrote about Kitchener, where I was born and spent the first 38 years of my life:

*The Elora Christmas Market, Elora, Ontario*

*Sunrise at Niagara Falls, view from my hotel*

*The drive to Thunder Bay, Ontario in the Fall*

*Lake Superior Provincial Park – this was the view from my campsite*

*Sleeping Giant as seen from the Terry Fox Memorial*

# Manitoba

In Manitoba I went to Winnipeg to meet my friend Nina, who owns HutK, one of the best home furnishing stores in Canada. We went next door to Yujiro Sushi, one of Canada’s 100 Best Restaurants (a great list to build itinerary around).

From there I went to Riding Mountain National Park, which was a stunningly beautiful place I want to explore more of.

*Riding Mountain National Park in the Fall*

# Saskatchewan

A preview clip of my YouTube video that I will one day maybe publish when I have free time to edit videos.

When I told people I was driving across the country, everyone complained about how long and flat Saskatchewan was – and I didn’t have that experience. I think this is a virtue of “you only see what you expect to see.” If you see Saskatchewan as a path between Alberta and Ontario, you are going to see it as a road.

I went to Grasslands Provincial Park, 200km south of Moosejaw. It’s a Dark Sky Park. They have cabins you can (and should) rent. Grasslands is stunning day and night. You can go horseback riding, hiking, and look at the stars.

*Yes, it really looks like this in real life*

# Alberta

I had meant to stay in Dinosaur Provincial Park, but do to some scheduling changes I had to move my camping stop and couldn’t get another reservation. It’s popular and looks beautiful. I pivoted my stop to Drumheller, Alberta – Canada’s dinosaur capital. I was stunned walking around, as there is dinosaur statue after dinosaur statue after dinosaur statue. There’s a dinosaur museum (sold out the day I was there, plan ahead!) The landscape is rugged hoodoos jutting out of the earth.

I then went to Banff, Alberta. Banff, and nearby Lake Louise, are some of the most popular tourist destinations in Canada. Banff is beautiful, set in between mountains on all sides and bursting with wildlife. I stayed in the Banff National Park campground and you can walk into the town of Banff. I missed Lake Louise as it was snowing for the first time of the year when I left Banff.

Near Banff is the town of Canmore, a now tourist destination set with the mountains in the background. Of course, there is also Calgary (and the Calgary Stampede), Edmonton, and a slew of small towns to explore.

*Drumheller has a surreal amount of dinosaur statues and a dinosaur museum*

*The town of Banff, next to Banff National Park, is a beautiful place to stay in the mountains*

The view from the Banff Sulphur Springs

British Columbia

While many people think of Vancouver first, British Columbia is a huge and diverse province. During my roadtrip, I drove through the mountains from Alberta to the coast, stopping in Kelowna to see a friend, then camping at Lake Okanagan in the middle of the mountain ranges. Kelowna and Lake Okanagan are in a stunning landscape that feels somewhere completely different than the rest of Canada, very Californian. The mountain drive is intense on both sides, particularly the Coquihalla highway.

I drove through Vancouver and took the ferry to Nanaimo (specifically to make Nanaimo Bars on video, yes) on Vancouver Island. I wish I would have spent more time on the island – driving through it was stunning. My friend Jacqui tells me I need to go to Tofino (“It is where my heart lives, Marko.”). Victoria was my last stop on the west coast of Canada and it was very cute.

From Jacqui: “Tofino is magic, I don’t know how else to describe it. Like fairies and mermaids and magic. And rainbows and butterflies and fresh salt air. And white sand and big trees and rainforests. And beautiful book stores and yummy coffee. And fresh seafood. And artists and art everywhere.”

Previously I’d been to Whistler for a conference. Many people think of Whistler for skiing, but it was stunningly beautiful to take the gondola to the top of the mountain and go for hikes along the beautiful views.

*Lake Okanagan South Campground*

*Lake Okanagan South Campground*

*Me, 10 years ago, at a conference in Whistler during the summer.*

*Whistler, British Columbia, in the summer*

*Victoria, British Columbia*

The True North, Strong and Free: Canada’s Territories

Canada also has 3 northern territories – I have not been to them, but my friends have. The Yukon, The Northwest Territories, and Nunavut. My friend lives in Yellowknife, NWT and shared the following:

The ‘Territory,’ as locals call it, is pure Canada: north, bitterly cold for 6 months of the year & immensely vast. Think Canadian Shield, trees, lakes, waterfalls and landscapes for as far as the eye can see. But don’t don’t forget it’s also full of kind, adventurous and resourceful Canadians - spread across 33-ish communities that dot its landscape. The largest community and the capital is Yellowknife, which is accessible via plane and car (only a short 15 hrs north from Edmonton).

Activities here are heavily season dependent. If you’re coming in the Winter (November-April), you can enjoy so many uniquely Canadian experiences (assuming you’ve got a parka and some warm boots). Imagine seeing the…

  • Northern lights. Yellowknife’s very clear skies give you the highest probability to see the Northern Lights in North America (and possibly the whole world). They are best seen Feb-May and Sept-October.
  • Winter activity paradise. Cross country ski across frozen lakes, snowshoe, skijor, sled dog, snowmobile.
  • March is all about the Snowking Ice Castle winter festival. Yes there’s a ice castle built on-top of Great Slave Lake, and yes there are comedy, music and movie nights hosted on many nights. Oh also, there’s ice slides - they are seriously slippy!
  • There is a ~10 km long ice road connecting Yellowknife to the nearby community of N’Dilo. Take a car, take a walk, or do both!
  • Get some freshly caught fish & chips at the famous Bullocks Restaurant. The vibe & aesthetic give the best hipster brunch spot anywhere in Canada a run for its money. There’s also the Woodyard & NWT Brewing Co. too with locally made beer & gin.

The summer has so much to offer as well. Imagine the best camping, canoeing, fishing, boating you can do in Canada but add the midnight sun and subtract any traffic or stress. Oh also, don’t sleep on Folk on the Rocks - it’s a very unique festival held just on the outskirts of Yellowknife every summer.

*Photo credit: Sam Legge*

*Photo credit: Sam Legge*

*Photo credit: Sam Legge*

*Photo credit: Sam Legge*

With Glowing Hearts

To make your travel plan, figure out what you love and work backwards to your plans in Canada. Canada has nearly everything to experience.

  • If you love theatre, head to Stratford, Ontario for the Stratford festival and build the rest of your trip around that.
  • If you love food, work backwards from the Top 100 Restaurants list or find a farm-to-table region like Annapolis Valley, Nova Scotia.
  • If you love history, head to Ottawa, St. Andrews By The Sea, or Annapolis Royal.
  • If you love the beach, take your pick of coasts – surf in Tofino, BC or Cow Bay, NS. Rent a cottage in Tobermory, Ontario. Tan on the red sand beaches of PEI.
  • If you love camping and hiking, head to any Canadian National or Provincial park. I’m heading to Cape Split in Nova Scotia this summer.
  • If you love city life, head to Toronto, Montreal, or Vancouver. At a smaller scale, Halifax, Winnipeg, Kitchener, Ottawa, Calgary, St. John, or St. John’s.
  • If you love a grand adventure, take the train to the Yukon or drive to Yellowknife and see the northern lights. Drive the Cabot Trail on Cape Breton Island. Head to the Magdalen Islands or Fogo Island. Drive through the mountain ranges of British Columbia.
  • If you love to go skiing or snowboarding (or just sitting by a fire), head to Whistler or Tremblant or Collingwood (or Wentworth in Nova Scotia).
  • If you want historic Christmas magic, head to Quebec City, or cute small towns like Elora.

My list is not complete. It’s biased based on my own life experiences and limited experiences through this big beautiful country.

Canada has something for everyone, every time of the year. Summers here are hot, Fall and Winter are stunningly beautiful in every province and territory.

It’s time for Canadians to discover what’s in our own backyard.

– Marko

item.title: Buy Canadian. Bye American.
item.description:
I am an advocate for buying Canadian at most times, but we are entering into an economic war with the United States, a war where the leader of the United States Government has publicly stated his goal is to annex our country.

It’s unacceptable.

I’m sad we are here. I’m proud that our country standing up for itself. I’m proud of how Trudeau framed this challenge. It’s going to get very hard economically.

Buying American at this stage means supporting a war against our own sovereignty as a nation. It sounds crazy to write down, but it’s been a crazy 12 days.

Pivoting how you spend money is expensive, time consuming, and annoying – you’re going to have to learn to cook very differently, very soon.

But it’s up to us to help our economy, especially if you are affluent. I’ve been buying Canadian for years. Here’s my advice.

Understand Made in Canada terminology

Corporations like to use marketing to confuse consumers. This will get worse in the coming weeks, and then it will quickly become clear what is actually made in Canada when counter-tariffs go into place.

You’ll hear things like “Canadian Owned” or “Proudly Canadian.” These words are bullshit, legally speaking.

The core phrases that are regulated are:

  • Product of Canada
  • Made in Canada

When shopping, one of these words will be on the product listing, packaging, or tag.

Do not trust the website that generically say “Proudly Canadian or “Canadian Heritage.” This is just branding and legally meaningless.

You need to look at each and every product you are buying.

For example, Reigning Champ used to be a premium, Canadian-made menswear brand. Aritizia (Canadian-owned) purchased them in 2021 and over the last few years then outsourced all manufacturing from British Columbia to Vietnam (while increasing prices). They did this slowly over their product lines, and now they no longer make products in Canada.

Stanfields is a well-known Canadian underwear brand, but only two of their mens products are made in Canada and the rest of their products are made in China.

You have to look at the tags in person, or the product listings online. If it’s made in Canada they will tell you loudly.

100% Canadian

100% of materials and labour are from Canada.

Product of Canada

98% of materials are Canadian sourced and Canadian manufactured.

  • A t-shirt is sewn in Canada and made with Canadian grown cotton that’s milled in Canada.
  • Ketchup is made with Canadian grown tomatoes and manufactured in a Canadian facility.

Made in Canada

51% of the direct costs of manufacture were in Canada. Components of the product are Canadian but it includes imported materials. It’s manufactured in Canada.

  • A t-shirt is sewn in Canada with American grown cotton that’s milled in Canada.
  • Hummus is made and packaged in Canada with imported ingredients.

Crafted in Canada / Assembled in Canada / Packaged in Canada / {Activity} In Canada

< 51% of the direct costs of manufacturing were in Canada, but some portion of processing was completed domestically.

  • A t-shirt is sewn in Canada with Malaysian cotton milled in Switzerland.
  • A car is assembled in Canada with Taiwanese chips and American components.
  • Protein powder is put into a plastic tub in Canada with the powder created elsewhere in the world.

“Designed in Canada”

This is not a regulated term. This is a very misleading term, it means the business headquarters is in Canada but the vast majority of employees are outside Canada, typically in Asia or Eastern Europe. You could have 2 employees in Canada and 100 in other countries.

There’s a small Canadian brand (I won’t name) that does this. They went so far as to write “Sustainable packaging 100% Made in Canada” on their product listing because the cardboard boxes they ship plates in are made in Canada. The plates themselves are not.

Be careful of snake oil salespeople during this time of patriotism.

“An Iconic Canadian Brand”

This is a very misleading view of the world:

  • Tim Horton’s is a Canadian icon that is owned by a Brazilian multinational.
  • Sleeman Breweries is owned by a Japanese multinational.
  • Labatt Brewing is owned by a Belgian multinational.

None of the money spent at these brands stays in Canada. We need to stop selling off Canadian wealth, but that’s a separate story.

If you buy coffee at a small coffee shop (or Second Cup) that money stays in Canada. If you buy Tim Horton’s it does not.

Imported – Not made in Canada, usually made in China if they do not list the country of origin.

Small Makers – Small makers, at farmers markets and craft fairs, often cannot legally make claims due to regulations. Ask them. If you’re at a farmers market, ask if they are a grower or a reseller. Being a small business is hard, I know this personally – help them survive this.

Move your online dollars

  • Subscribe to CBC Gem and Crave instead of Netflix, Amazon Prime, Disney+ and Apple TV+
  • Hold off on buying a new phone or computer
  • Cancel Meta – Meta has proactively allowed hate speech policies against LGBTQ people
  • Stop using Amazon Prime and go shop at a locally owned store even though its much more work – Amazon also removed their LGBTQ worker protections and equity for Black people; they pulled out of Quebec to stop a union

Stop subscribing to American-owned Canadian news sources

Post Media, 66% of which is owned by an American private equity firm, has purchased the majority of Canadian news sites including:

  • The National Post
  • The Financial Post
  • The Toronto Sun
  • Almost every single local newspaper / publisher, list here

Cancel your subscriptions to American-owned Canadian news. Focus on CBC News, or the Bell/Telus/Rogers owned media properties.

You might say “Oh no, our local paper will go away!” It’s already gone away, they just regurgitate what headquarters pushes onto their websites. Start a community paper.

This is going to get very expensive: stop shopping at the big box stores to save money

Big box stores are convenient, they are also a rip-off.

  • Produce and meat are likely going to go up 25% in price
  • Learn to make delicious, cost effective meals with produce we grow locally – try my Ugly Vegetable Winter recipes (PDF book) because it’s cabbage season until May
  • Learn how to make cost effective, high protein, delicious meals with dry beans
  • Find local, independently owned grocery, and hardware stores

Farmers Markets are your friend

I wrote a whole guide on how to shop at farmer’s markets.

I recently moved to rural Nova Scotia, and here the Wolfville Farmer’s Market offers an option where you can shop online and do pick-up in your rural community. Even in rural Nova Scotia, I can buy 95% of my groceries at the farmers market, directly from Canadian producers – meat, vegetables, fruit, milk, cheese, snacks, etc.

Yes, in winter it’s hard. I have been making a lot of apple based desserts and a lot of roasted cabbage. But that’s what we grow in Canada.

We’re in for a very harsh lesson on what is grown here. Learn to make the most of it.

Stop vacationing in the US, vacation in Canada

I just drove across the country. Canada is beautiful. Spend your money here.

  • Visit the Canadian National and Provincial Parks, I particularly loved Riding Mountain in Manitoba and Lake Okanagan.
  • Visit the Maritimes, they are insanely beautiful and have so much to offer.

Look at who owns the hotel chains. None of the large chains are owned by Canadians. Stay at smaller, locally owned inns and B&Bs.

Make an inventory of where your money is going

Look at your debit and credit card statements. Make a list of what you’re buying and who owns those companies. Take time when you are shopping to pivot.

  • Groceries → You will have to change your diet, if only because of the cost of meat and produce going up at least 25% after this. Use this opportunity to shop local.
  • Beer and Wine → Canada has so many great producers. Start going directly to breweries and wineries, so many of their products are not available in the Provincial liquor stores. Many have online stores and ship.
  • Household → There are many Canadian producers, as you pick up toilet paper, paper towel, cleaning products, etc. search for lists of providers.
  • Hardware → Immediately move from Home Depot and Lowes to Home Hardware
  • Entertainment → Cut streaming, use CBC Gem and Crave; sign up at your local library (they have everything)
  • Clothing → There are so many great Canadian-made brands at various price-points. I personally shop on the bougier side and love brands like Okay To Rest, House of Blanks, 18Waits, Anian, Outclass, and Province of Canada, but I recognize these brands are pricier than others (but the quality is great).

There are also amazing rural Canadians with terrible websites, like PEI knitters who make great sweaters, or wool duvets made in the prairies, you can buy towels made in Canada. If you need it, it’s probably made here.

Find more options and ask questions on the Buy Canadian subreddit.

If you are a business owner, move your service providers

Business owners have more capacity for capital movement than individuals. If you are a business owner, look at moving from American providers to Canadian providers.

If you make a packaged product, move to a Canadian provider. If you provide digital services, move to a Canadian provider. If you need professional services, move to a Canadian provider.

More than any individual, you can move millions of dollars back into the Canadian economy.

As an employee, ask your COO or CFO how much capital goes to American service providers.

Do not move from American-owned to Chinese-owned

China is not a friend of Canada. We need to invest into countries where their governments support the same value system as Canadians. If the Charter of Rights and Freedoms conflicts with the government in power, don’t support them.

My personal value system is to purchase first from countries where I have the right to get married and women have as equal rights to men as is possible within a patriarchal society. Human rights are expensive.

Follow your own value system. Apply it to where you spend your money.

Remember this is about a government, not a people

Americans are still our friends. The current American government is not.

I know you are busy and tired and overwhelmed, but do it anyway.

Once you make it a habit of looking at who owns a company and where products are made, it becomes second nature. You flip over a bottle, you pop open that hidden drawer on a website. It takes seconds.

Google “Who owns X” (then Google who owns them until you work your way up the chain).

Starting this habit is hard.

Now is the time.

Take care of your neighbours

This is going to hit people hard economically and emotionally.

If you have the time, mental capacity, emotional capacity, or financial capacity, help your neighbours get through this.

Be kind to each other.

Together we’re strong.

– Marko

item.title: Cheesy, Tomato Pasta Bake
item.description:
This is an easy, pantry-based weeknight recipe I recently made. It tastes like lasagna with substantially less effort.

You can skip baking this to save on time and dishes, but the crispy cheese moments are worth it.

Ingredients

Marcella Hazan’s Tomato Sauce

  • 1 x 28-ounce can of tomatoes (get Bianco di Napoli at Vincenzo’s if in KW)
  • 1 onion, peeled, cut in half
  • 5 tablespoons butter
  • 1 tsp salt

Turkey

  • 2-3 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 medium onion, chopped
  • 1 clove of garlic, finely chopped
  • 1lb ground turkey
  • Salt and pepper

Pasta and assembly

  • 1lb pasta (I used orichiette)
  • 250g ricotta
  • 100g cheddar cheese, cut into cubes
  • 50g parmesan cheese, finely grated

Method

Make the tomato sauce

Put the canned tomatoes, peeled onion halves, butter, and salt into a 3-quart pot on medium-low for 45 minutes, until the tomatoes are soft, and the butter has embedded into the tomatoes, with some oil visible on the surface.

This is a great, low effort sauce to make anytime you want a red sauce.

Brown the turkey

In a 12” oven safe frying pan with high sides (like a cast iron or braiser), heat the olive oil on medium-high. Add the onion and a pinch of salt, cook until soft, 5-10 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant (don’t burn it). Add the turkey, season with salt and pepper, cook until browned outside and cooked through.

Add the tomato sauce to the turkey.

You can use ground beef, pork, chicken, vegan protein, whatever you want here. We just had turkey in the freezer to use.

Assemble & bake

Note: If you don’t have a large enough frying pan to go in the oven, assemble everything in a 13x9” baking dish.

Pre-heat oven to 425°F.

Boil your pasta per the instructions on the packaging. Add 1/2 cup pasta water to the tomato sauce (the starches in the pasta water help it have a nice texture). Drain the pasta and add to your pan with the sauce and turkey.

Add half the ricotta and cheddar in little drops around the pan and lightly stir into the pasta. Top with 1 tsp sized dollops of ricotta and cheddar, then grate parmesan all over the top.

Place pan (or baking dish) in the oven for ~20 minutes until the top is very golden brown and bubbling. Keep an eye on it as baking times might vary depending how hot everything is when you assemble it. You want those crispy cheese moments at the edges that taste like lasagna.

item.title: Cookbook Supper Club
item.description:
As I pack up my life and get ready to move in just over two weeks, I’m reflecting a lot on what I want to keep in my life and what I want to get rid of. While this evaluation is happening for relationships, emotions, and memories, it’s also happening for a lot of physical stuff.

Moving, particularly moving your life into storage you have to pay for, forces you to confront what you think you value, and what you actually value.

After 11 years in the same house, I’ve collected a lot of stuff I thought I cared about at some point.

I’m not much of a hoarder, but I’ve often left more emotionally difficult things to deal with later. Things I can hide it in the basement. But in a few weeks I’ll no longer have a basement. I won’t have any home at all.

My stuff is going to a few places, broadly categorized as:

  1. Things I need on a two month long camping trip where I will film a cooking show in the woods with a kitchen powered by my electric truck.
  2. Things that need a human, like plants.
  3. Things I want in Nova Scotia for an indeterminate amount of time until I have a house, like shoes and my Peloton bike, that need a temporary home.
  4. Things I need to build a house, like my chop saw and drills, that need a temporary home.
  5. Things I need once I have a house, like my couch, which I am paying to put into climate controlled storage and have driven out to Nova Scotia once I have a place to live. But I might not see these things for 2 years! And it’s very expensive!

As I work through my material possessions, I’m finding many things get to the bottom of this flowchart and I have to ask myself: do I really want to pay to store this for two years until I have a house again? Is it not cheaper to simply buy it again instead? Am I going to unpack this in two years only to take it somewhere to donate it?

So, I am getting rid of a lot of stuff right now.

Some of these decisions are easy. I have 15 years of Bon Appetit magazines. I don’t need them. I found a good home for them.

But when it comes to my kitchen, each question becomes a lot harder. Well, I might need my blender before I have a house (I might need it in the woods!). And what do I do with all these cookbooks? I might need them! In the woods!

You see, I love cookbooks.

I love the unique personality of them – the design, the writing, the photos. I love how they tell stories. I love trying out the recipes and putting my own little star rating inside the book. I love how you can tell a cookbook written for the author, and a cookbook written for a marketable audience. I love going back to cookbooks at different times of the year, over the years.

I have a list of my favourite cookbooks on my website. (I wrote this two years ago and it is not current).

The problem with loving cookbooks, buying cookbooks, and collecting cookbooks is that you rarely get to work your way through them. Many have 100+ recipes, and often you only make a handful. Some cookbooks, like Dessert Person by Claire Saffitz, are amazing reference manuals – I’ve made nearly every recipe. Dessert Person is always on my counter, and is probably coming on my road trip.

Some cookbooks, like Six Seasons, I like to use as inspiration – a jumping off point. And others, like Notes From a Small Kitchen Island, or anything by Nigel Slater, I adore the writing in, but haven’t made too many recipes – my most made recipe from Notes From a Small Kitchen Island is for dog biscuits (5/5 tail wags). I just haven’t had the capacity to try too many others, as it competes with all the other cookbooks in my home.

I’ve always wanted a way to try more recipes from a cookbook, without, say, eating from Mi Cocina every day for a month (which I did, I love that book). And often, I want to try the super complicated project recipes, like mole, which is a large thing to do for a single person.

So while I haven’t yet figured out what to do with all my cookbooks, I have figured out how to get the most out of them.

My favourite way to explore a cookbook is Cookbook Supper Club.

Two years ago my friend Jordan, who at the time I only knew as the owner of Legacy Greens, asked if I would like to attend a cookbook supper club with her and her friends.

I had no idea what this was, so I said yes.

I was very pretty nervous about joining, I didn’t know anyone there, and at the time I really only knew Jordan from shopping at her store. That first cookbook club night, and every one since, has been wonderful.

I’ve made great new friends. I’ve tried so much delicious new food that I never would have had or made before. Cookbook club has since become one of my favourite parts of every month.

Cookbook club is something I am going to take with me – to make a Nova Scotia branch of it. And it’s the kind of thing I think you could try, too.

What is cookbook club?

Our version of cookbook club is a group of 5–10 people who all love food, cooking, and each other’s company. It’s a flexible group, as not everyone can make it each month, and people come and go with the seasons of their lives. There’s a core group, but this club is a branch from a previous cookbook club! Sometimes we have five people, sometimes we have newcomers as guests. It’s always fun.

Each month someone volunteers to host dinner. That person selects a cookbook and shares the recipe list. Everyone picks a recipe, makes it, and brings it to the host’s house – generally potluck / family style. We share a meal together, catch up on life, and it’s pretty great!

We’ve got a good rhythm – I usually make something complicated. Nick always makes surprise bread or desserts. Jordan brings fun beverages from Legacy Greens (I am convinced this is how she does market research now). Sarah usually has some secret career, like shearing sheep, that she tells us about. Misha has made her outfit in addition to what she has made for dinner.

We all cheer each other on. We also have very great conversations, sometimes about butter, but mostly about our lives.

If you want to start your own cookbook supper club, my advice is below.

Make it easy to share recipes

We use WhatsApp for our group chat. It also has a handy polling feature for figuring out dates.

Once the host picks a book, they send photos of the recipe list. Most cookbooks will have either a global list of recipes at the start of the book, or a per-chapter list of recipes. We’ll usually bring the physical cookbook to dinner. Sometimes (meaning, once) we were prepared enough to bring the next cookbook to dinner to peruse.

Sometimes specific recipes stand out. More often, the group will make requests like:

  • “I only have time to make a simple salad or side dish”
  • “I’d like something that’s a complicated project”
  • “I want to make a dessert”

And then the host, who physically has the cookbook, can peruse more in detail to send out some options. The host typically tries to balance the appetizers, entrees, and desserts, but if we end up with all entrees we just roll with it.

After doing this for a while I have a few tips:

  • If you’re hosting, take your cookbook to a well lit room, place it on a table, and hold it flat so there isn’t glare on the pages.
  • If you’re reading recipes, on most phones you can select text from photos – just press-and-hold the recipe text on the photo and you can copy/paste the text into your favourite notes or recipe app!

### There are always sneaky secret recipes

As the host, you need to read the ingredients list and not blindly send recipes.

Cookbook authors are sneaky, they will make a recipe look simpler by listing elements of the recipe like this:

  • 1 batch of peach filling (page 134)
  • 1 pie crust (page 172)
  • 1 recipe of whipped cream (page 84)

And you think you’ve sent the whole recipe, but you have not!

And because we are all flawed human beings who won’t actually read the recipe until the day before cookbook club, we will then panic and ask for all of these secret recipes that were hidden in the ingredients lists. This also means as a person cooking, you should read the recipe a week before in case you need to marinate or hydrate something, go to a special store, or ask for a sneaky secret recipe!

Be true to yourselves, not the cookbook

Usually every cookbook club Jordan will say “The recipe said to buy this, and that, and this other thing. But I didn’t want to do that, so I used this instead.” We love and support Jordan for who she is.

In our cookbook club we prioritize being together, having fun, and trying something new over following the rules.

Everyone has different schedules, budgets, and access to ingredients.

At the end of the day, if you can’t find an ingredient, do a reasonable swap. You don’t need to go to 14 stores and spend $75 on spices you’ll never use again. Speciality ingredients usually can be shared – check with the group chat – so if you need to buy smoked black cardamom, maybe somebody else needs it too and you can share it. You can even do a field trip to specialty stores together!

Recipes aren’t rules, they are ideas. For our club, the goal is fun and togetherness.

Sarah Describes a Pancake

Sarah Flambés a Pancake

Present your dishes

We usually go around the table at the start of dinner, each person discusses what they made, the challenges they had with ingredients, how cooking went. It’s generally pretty funny.

Sometimes there’s a performance (see the video of Sarah’s flambé, above), sometimes it’s the surprising delight of a dish (I made a peach tarte tatin that didn’t survive the evening), or a different ingredient (lamb liver mousse) or technique. Sometimes we just like the name (“Fitness Salad” and “Relish of the Seven Lucky Gods”).

Help clean up

After dinner, we all help clean up – even when the host protests (me). If the host is uncomfortable with accepting help, focus on washing your own dishes to take home and use them to pack your leftovers!

For the hosts:

  • If you don’t have enough dishes or cutlery, ask someone in the club to bring some over
  • People will usually need serving tools for their dishes, if you don’t have enough ask folks to bring some over
  • Often people will need to finish their recipes at your house, for our last cookbook I made a peach tarte tatin. I had to roll out my puff pastry, assemble, and bake at Sarah’s house – so I had to ask Sarah to leave me some countertop and oven space.
  • Try to balance the menu between appetizers, entrées, and desserts; but also using your stove and oven. Fresh salads and pre-made desserts really help here!

For the guests:

  • Bring containers for leftovers (you can also pack in your serving dish!). There are always so many leftovers.
  • Try to bring everything you need for your dish, if you need something specific let the host know in advance.
  • If you have to finish preparing your dish at the host’s house, let them know – especially if you need stove or oven space!
  • Read your recipe in advance, sometimes you are missing pages of a recipe, or it references another recipe, or something had to be started 1-2 in advance. Sometimes you need a specialty ingredient you need to track down or order online!
  • Bring a small gift for the host. I usually bring something homemade. Once I brought Misha a lemon that I grew in my home gym!
  • Bring drinks that you want to share.

That’s all there really is to Cookbook Club.

It’s fun. It brings me joy. Cookbook Club is full of such lovely relationships, emotions, and memories I am going to take with me when I move. I’m going to start a new chapter of Cookbook Club, and I hope the KW crew will come visit me for a Cookbook Club Road Trip.

# FAQs

Much like cookbooks and recipes themselves, this is how we do cookbook club. You can use this to inspire how you do cookbook club. Our goal is fun and community, not strictly following rules or recipes.

How do I choose the right cookbook for the club?

Pick a cookbook you like, even if you’ve never used it before. If the recipes are terrible, they are terrible, and everyone bonds over it. That is part of the adventure!

Should the meals be themed or follow specific chapters of the cookbook?

You can! We haven’t. As long as the recipes are in the cookbook we consider them fair game, and we don’t really focus on if the dishes go together (generally they do).

How many members should be in the supper club?

We have 10 people in the group, usually 5–7 attend. We keep it going even if people can’t join, otherwise it’s too easy for the whole thing to fall apart. Sarah is really the one who makes this happen. You need a leader.

How often should the club meet?

We meet once a month! Your club might vary!

How much time does it take?

Usually we set the invitation for 6pm. People trickle in. We chat, catch up, finish preparing our recipes, set the table. This usually takes around an hour. We eat, we have dessert, we help clean up, and everyone’s gone by 9 or 10pm.

Where should the supper club meetings be held?

Someone volunteers to be the host each month, and we ask for that at the end of each cookbook club. We don’t have a schedule more than a month out. We rotate between who is hosting. You could also have a fixed host. It’s your club, make your own rules!

What are some tips for organizing the first meeting?

How do I find people to join?

Ask the people in your life who like food! They don’t have to be crazy home cooks or super foodies. Most people love the idea. Keep it simple.

“I saw this post about hosting a cookbook supper club – everyone gets together and brings a different dish from the same cookbook. I thought it sounded fun. Would you be interested in trying that?”

How do we handle dietary restrictions or food allergies among members?

We are lucky in that we don’t have any dietary restrictions or allergies in our club. If you do, you’ll want to make sure remind everyone of this at every planning chat, particularly if you’re inviting new people.

If you have a crew with fairly specific needs, like gluten free, dairy free, vegan, I’d suggest focusing on cookbooks, cuisines, and recipes that fit those dietary needs. You can also be discerning on which recipes get included.

If someone does have a known allergen, and you are going to use an ingredient they are allergic to, make it known. Make sure to have extra serving ware available so as not to cross-contaminate food.

You can usually swap out ingredients.

When it comes to food preferences – not allergies – it’s important to set those aside. We’re often doing cookbooks from a wide variety of geographic and cultural areas, we’re often trying new ingredients and flavours. If that’s not something you enjoy, cookbook supper club may not be for you.

What is the best way to split the costs of ingredients?

For our club, everyone is responsible for their own dish. You’re in charge of the recipe you select for yourself. You choose how much time and money you want to spend. You buy your own ingredients.

You are not in charge of other people’s decisions or budgets. If you feel you’re putting in more comparative effort, you can choose to put in less effort by picking a different recipe. The recipe is your choice.

This has never been an issue in our club. I’m often using organic ingredients, finding obscure speciality ingredients, and doing things like making a 35 ingredient mole because that is how I have fun. I don’t expect that from anyone else.

You can certainly take a different approach, such as setting budgets, but it’s so much easier and less drama if everyone chooses what is accessible to their interest, skills, schedule, and budget.

How do we maintain a balance between recipes?

Everyone picks their own dish. You can try to encourage a balance appetizers, entrees, and desserts as people select their dishes. In our club, the self selection process works really well, with people adjusting based on whoever picks their recipe first.

Should the supper club include drinks, and if so, how do we decide on pairings?

You can make this as simple or complicated as you want to.

For our club, generally everyone brings something. I usually bring a non-alcoholic option as I don’t usually drink. We don’t do pairings. You might, but that takes a lot of extra planning!

How do we encourage discussion about the food and the cookbook?

The host often has spent the most time with the cookbook (though sometimes multiple people have the book). It’s great when the host can share how they found the book, some fun facts about the author. Everyone shares their experience making their recipe.

What should be done if someone can't attend?

This happens a lot, and often at the last minute. We just go on anyway. Once we only had four people and it was the funniest, spiciest cookbook club.

Should the club have a leader or rotate responsibilities among members?

Sarah is our de facto leader. If she doesn’t herd the cats, we don’t get together. She sends out reminders, calendar invites, and polls.

We are all very grateful for Sarah. Be the Sarah you want to see in the world.

How do we document our experience?

We keep it simple. Sarah has a Google doc with all the books we’ve done. We take photos of all the food and post it in the group chat. Sometimes I bring my camera! Sometimes I don’t!

You can make it more complex, but that’s what we do!

*My first ever Cookbook Club – “Family Recipes” – where I brought my cabbage recipe and Sarah brought her dad.*

*And here we are, almost two years later, with Cookbook Club helping to paint my house before I put it up for sale earlier this year!*

item.title: Buying an electric vehicle
item.description:
I bought a Rivian R1T Adventure!

It’s an electric pick-up truck with a large battery!

I’ve had it for just over a week as I write this post. I really like it so far. I’ve learned so much in the process of buying an electric vehicle (EV). I personally had so many questions before the purchase, and so many people have me asked questions since.

This post is meant to organize my thoughts for easy access to information, for anyone considering an EV.

*I went camping on Sunday at The Pinery, an Ontario Provincial Park, to test out my camping setup – I bought an iKamper Sky Camp Mini 3.0 hardshell roof top tent for my cross country trip.*

I also want to share this as there is a lot of misinformation around EVs – online, at dealerships, at dinner tables. This is partly because the vehicles available and charging infrastructure has changed a lot in the last few years, and partly because dealerships are disincentivized to sell EVs. Having that, almost every automaker has great EVs now (there is a list at the end of this post).

This is a very long post. The short version is that today, EVs are a great choice for most people – if you have the budget for one. As long as this post is, EVs are quite simple to own and drive.

Why are there so many kinds of electric vehicles now?

When you are shopping for an EV, there are many confusing terms as traditional automakers are trying to market internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles as EVs.

The following types of vehicles use only electricity to drive the vehicle:

  • BEV: Battery Electric Vehicle. This is what you think of when you hear EV. These are pure electric vehicles like Rivian and Tesla, the Ford Mustang Mach-E, Volkswagen id.4, Hyundai Ioniq, etc. Most new BEVs with extended range batteries have ~500km (300 miles) of range on a full charge. You can recharge at EV charging stations or at home. The entire thing is electric, there is no gas. BEVs have the largest Federal rebates available. This post is going to focus mostly on BEVs.

The following types of vehicles are gas vehicles with supplemental electric motors and batteries, and only some types of these vehicles can use electricity to drive the car for a limited range. Because these vehicles have gas engines, they require all of the maintenance of ICE vehicles (like oil changes and buying gas).

  • PHEV: Plug-In Hybrid Electric Vehicle. These vehicles have a small electric motor and battery, usually providing 20–40km of pure electric range, and then a gas engine that drives like a typical car. You can recharge at EV charging stations or at home. When the battery runs out it switches to a gas engine, which you can fill up at any gas station. You basically have two cars in one. These are for people who mostly drive in the city and can’t move past their range anxiety for longer trips. PHEVs have smaller Federal rebates available.
  • Hybrid: Hybrids, like the Toyota Prius, also have a small electric motor and battery. This battery is even smaller than in a PHEV, and its main goal is to support the engine – boosting power and torque, and at city driving speeds it can power the vehicle with only electricity. The battery also supplies power to heating, cooling, and infotainment systems to increase fuel efficiency. Since the battery is small, it is only charged by regenerative braking – you can’t plug it in. This is old technology, the first Prius came out in 1997!
  • MHEV: Mild Hybrid Electric Vehicle. These have an even smaller battery and motor, powered by regenerative braking. MHEVs use regenerative braking to create electricity that takes the full load off the engine, increasing fuel efficiency, but you can’t drive in an all electric mode. This is purely a marketing term and in my opinion these really shouldn’t be branded as EVs. They are much more fuel efficient, I rented a Volvo XC90 Mild Hybrid in April and got 800km of range with a 40L tank of gas. But at the end of the day, it’s a more efficient gas vehicle.

Only BEVs and PHEVs are eligible for the Canadian Federal iZEV rebate program. The rebate takes $2,500 (PHEV) to $5,000 (BEV) from the after-tax cost of an EV at the point of sale (you save the money at the dealership, not your tax return). You can view eligible vehicles here. Some Provinces also have additional incentives for BEVs (not Ontario).

Before diving any further in, a note on terminology below: when I refer ICE vehicles – internal combustion engine – I am referring to regular gas cars, SUVs, trucks, etc. When I refer to EVs after this point, I specifically mean Battery Electric Vehicles, as the hybrid options (PHEV, Hybrid, MHEV) do not share all the same features/benefits, and retain the same downsides as an ICE vehicle.

*While I was on my test camp, I powered my electric coffee grinder and electric kettle with the 120V/15A outlet in the truck bed to make pour over coffee in the morning. Why buy an EV?

There are many pros to buying an EV.

  • BEVs are nearly silent to drive, it’s a much more calming driving experience than an internal combustion engine (ICE).
  • BEVs are very fun to drive (even the lower cost ones) due to the way electric motors work. They zoom! They’re smooth!
  • BEVs have fewer parts that can break. The entire vehicle is a battery, one or more electric motors, two axles, an HVAC system, and many computers. There are ~20 moving components in an EV that can break and over 2,000 in an ICE vehicle.
  • BEVs have almost zero maintenance costs. You have to change your air filter and maintain your tires/brakes. That’s it. ICE vehicles need regular maintenance, like oil changes. BEVs don’t need oil.
  • Daily operating costs for a BEV are far lower than the cost of operating an ICE vehicle. To drive 100km, it will cost you ~$0.20 with EV if you charge at home, ~$2.00 if you charge at a commercial charger. A relatively efficient ICE vehicle will cost ~$15 if regular gas to drive 100km (at 8L/100km performance).
  • Car insurance is cheaper for EVs (green vehicle discounts).
  • EVs with Green license plates can use the HOV lane in Ontario with only one occupant (your State/Province might vary).

  • EVs have a ton of bonus perks since they are giant batteries:

    • Some EVs have 15A electrical outlets (the same as in your home), so you can plug things into it – like an induction cooktop, electric kettle, and a countertop oven, or use power tools.
    • Some EVs have “Camp Mode” where the HVAC system will stay on overnight if you camp inside the vehicle.
    • Today, vehicles like the Ford F150 Lightning (and, allegedly soon for Rivian) have Vehicle-to-Home Power. This means during a blackout, your vehicle’s battery can power your house. Depending on your battery size and how much power you use, this could power a single family home for over a week – great if you live in places prone to storms or unstable energy grids.
    • In the apocalypse you can power your car with a solar panel instead of siphoning expired gas while the zombies are coming for you! And with 0–60 in 3.5 seconds, you’ll get out of the zombies path fast!

There are so many ports

EVs need to support both Direct Current (DC power) for fast charging, and Alternating Current (AC power) for home charging. This is important to know for how you evaluate charging stations, plugs, and adapters.

Today EV charging is a bit like smartphones in 2011. Does your phone have Mini USB? Micro USB? Lightning? Now everyone, even Apple, has a USB-C port on their phone (though some of us still have lightning ports). It’s like that.

EV Charging is in the middle of resolving that mess. You will see the following types of charging ports:

  • NACS (Tesla Supercharger) – This is the USB-C of EV charging. It’s the newly agreed upon North American Charging Standard for DC fast charging, designed by Tesla. Every manufacturer has agreed to move to NACS in North America. If you do not currently have a NACS vehicle, you can buy an adapter to convert from NACS → CSS. (Europe standardized on CCS1, and forced Tesla to adopt it).
  • CCS1 – Most non-Tesla vehicles on the market today have CCS ports. Most non-Tesla commercial charging stations have CCS plugs. If you have a NACS vehicle, you can purchase a CCS → NACS adapter to use CCS chargers.
  • J1772 – This is a smaller part of CCS, but for AC charging (home power). To use Tesla Destination Chargers you need a NACS → J1772 adapter.
  • ChAdeMo – This was an early type of plug that has mostly been discontinued. You’ll see it on older models like the Nissan Leaf, and some charging stations. It’s important to know insofar as you’ll say “what’s that?!” at charging stations and on maps.

If you buy a non-Tesla vehicle today, it most likely has a CCS charger. You’ll want to purchase a NACS → CCS adapter. All of the automakers have agreed to move to NACS, which will begin happening in 2026 model years or later.

Yes it's all confusing to read, but you buy an adapter once and you’re fine.

What’s all this about only charging to 80%?

There are a lot of myths and half-truths around EV charging that have become popularized. It’s all pretty complicated because it has to do with science and chemistry. The worries are very overblown.

Here is a scientific paper if you want to argue with people on the internet.

There are two main kinds of batteries in BEVs today. Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC) and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP, or LiFePO). NMC batteries use more rare earth metals, are more expensive, and smaller. LFP batteries are larger, heavier, and cheaper. There are newer battery technologies coming, but probably not for 10 years.

Batteries degrade over time, meaning they hold less charge – like how an iPhone starts dying by 8pm after 3 or 4 years. There are many factors that affect this.

LFP batteries are supposed to have very little degradation when charging to 100%, and can withstand 3,000-6,000 charge cycles before they lose noticeable performance. This would mean charging your vehicle from 0% to 100% every single day for 8–16 years!

NMC batteries will lose performance faster than LFP batteries when they are charged to the edges, meaning if you charge above 90% and run below 10% most of the time. When charging from 0 to 100%, your battery performance will fall within 450 charge cycles. If you keep charge between 20% and 80%, your performance will fall within 1,500 charge cycles.

While 450 charge cycles sounds low, 450 charge cycles from 0 to 100%, at 500km range for a full charge, is the equivalent of driving 225,000km. That’s around the lifecycle of an ICE vehicle’s engine. I don’t think anyone would expect an ICE vehicle to operate at peak performance after 225,000km (140,000 miles). Having said that, maintaining your battery between 20% and 80% will extend its capacity well into 450,000km – likely beyond the useful life of the vehicle.

Battery temperature also has a large impact on degradation, so try to pre-condition (warm up) your battery before fast charging as often as you can.

I’m personally not going to worry about it too much. If you want rules to follow, the basic guidelines most manufacturers, scientists, and strangers on the internet agree on are:

  • Try to stay between 20% and 80% most of the time.
  • Only plug in when you need to charge.
  • Only charge to 100% when you have to do very long drives where charging opportunities may be difficult to find, such as rural road trips.
  • Try not to let the battery fully die.
  • Pre-condition before charging.

Okay but what about the winter?

Newer EVs have battery conditioning technology, which is fancy for it uses a heater to warm up the battery to increase battery performance. Batteries operate better, with less degradation (caused by crystals forming) when they are warm. If you are charging your car at home, you can have it automatically condition the battery before you leave!

But I heard the range tanks as soon as it gets cold outside?

EVs lose the same range as ICE vehicles.

Generally, EV range seems to drop 15% as temperatures go below freezing. If you have 500km of range, you can expect 425km of range below freezing. With a conditioned (warmed up) battery, or vehicles with a heat pump, you will see a much lower drop – if any.

As a point of comparison, ICE vehicles lose 15% in efficiency/range at -6°C, and drop more than 25% in efficiency/range for short trips where the engine has no time to warm up. You won’t see this discussed as a reason not to buy gas vehicles – yet you’re fueling up your car more often, and spending more on gas in the winter!

No, someone told me that EVs just stop working if it’s cold!

EVs have the same operating temperature range as ICE vehicles.

EVs will likely not operate at all below -27°C (I mean, I will also stop operating at -27°C. It’s never been that cold here.)

Generally, ICE vehicles will also stop operating at this temperature. The battery may not start the engine, and the oil may be too thick for the engine to function (and turning it on could cause permanent damage to the engine!).

If it is -27°C you should stay home.

But someone told me if the battery dies the vehicle will never work again and I’ll have to spend thousands of dollars to have it towed!

If your EV battery dies on the road, you have a few options:

  • You can call service that offers “Vehicle to Vehicle” or “Vehicle to Load” (V2L charging. This can add 40km of range to get you to a charging station.
  • You can tow your vehicle to a charging station.
  • You can buy CAA. CAA Premier is $149/year, which includes 5 service calls per year. They provide emergency V2L charging, plus 320km of emergency towing once, and up to 200km of emergency towing 4 times. All for $149/year! Which is like, 5% of your fuel cost savings!

Any vehicle can receive V2L charging. Not all vehicles can provide power, though (Hyundai and Kia can). In the future, V2L will become a standard feature – which means other drivers will be able to give you a boost on the road in an emergency!

EV infrastructure has come a long way in the last five years. The issues early Tesla drivers faced aren’t really problems anymore.

But honestly, just take some of your fuel cost savings and buy CAA if you’re worried.

In older EV models, the battery completely draining did cause problems, since without a battery the vehicle can’t start the computers needed to regulate charging. But that was years ago. Most EVs now have a software-locked battery buffer (meaning, “100%” is actually 90%) and 12V battery to prevent this situation.

What’s this about regenerative braking? What is single pedal driving?

In a gas car, when you press down on the gas pedal you are accelerating the vehicle. If you let go of the gas pedal, the car will keep its momentum going until you hit the brake. When you press the brake, you are applying friction to the wheels to stop the vehicle. You have two pedals: one is go, one is stop.

Energy can’t be created or destroyed, only moved. When you brake a vehicle, you are moving energy. In traditional braking the energy moves in the form of heat generated by the brakes.

Regenerative Braking

EVs use a technology called regenerative braking. Instead of turning all of the energy from breaking into heat, some of that energy turns into electricity. Instead of using friction to stop the vehicle, your motor turns into a power generator that slows the vehicle’s momentum.

Single Pedal Driving

To increase how much power can be captured, EVs use an optional technique called single pedal driving to increase regenerative braking’s capacity to return energy. Single pedal driving can increase range by as much as 5% (~25km)!

It’s a really different driving experience.

With single pedal driving, the gas pedal acts more like a speed setting. If your foot isn’t on the accelerator, the car is stopped. If you press it down gently it will go 30km/h and stay there. If you press it down more it will go 50km/h and stay there. If you press it down firmly it will rapidly accelerate to 100km/h and stay there. If you don’t change the position of your foot it will keep that speed, as if cruise control is on. When you lift your foot off the pedal, the car will begin to brake until it stops.

Without pressing the brake.

If you test drive an EV this takes some getting used to. You can ask the car dealership to disable single pedal driving for your first test drive, so that the abrupt change in driving style doesn’t impact your view of the vehicle. Rivian, Ford, VW, and Tesla have buttery smooth implementations of single pedal driving, while Nissan and Honda feel like it’s your first day in driving school if you so much as wiggle your big toe.

The main risk with a used EV is battery degradation.

Yes – EV batteries may degrade after years depending how they are charged (see above).

You can, and should, ask a used car dealership to run battery diagnostics for you – you may even be able to do it yourself within the vehicle (Google “view battery health vehicle model” for instructions). You will also see accurate range estimates on the vehicle screen. To figure out max range, it’s simple math – divide the estimated range by the %.

  • If the vehicle has 30% battery left, and says 160km of range, divide 160 by 0.30.
  • 130/0.33 = 533km range at 100% charge!

Reduce your risk with a trust but verify approach:

  • Ask for a battery health report: if they don’t provide this, don’t buy the vehicle. Do your own math on the range based on the vehicle’s estimates.
  • Ask for a CarFax report: if they don’t provide this, don’t buy the vehicle.
  • Don’t trust the CarFax report: explicitly ask if the vehicle has any unreported damage, any repair history, any service, recalls, or parts replaced. Ask this over email so it is in writing. A friend bought a used ICE vehicle recently and they only disclosed an accident after he signed the contract, when he went to pick up the vehicle. You can imagine how that went.
  • Ask if the manufacturer’s warranty is still valid and transfers to a second owner. I called Rivian prior to purchase and provided them with the VIN to verify the warranty was still valid and would be transfer. You have to call to transfer the warranty, it is not automatic! This is true for Rivian, Tesla, Ford, VW, etc.
  • Test everything: door seals, sound systems, automatic locks, hard acceleration, hard braking, all the built-in cameras. You may only be able to do this on a second test drive, when you’re serious about that specific vehicle.

I bought my R1T at Shift Motors. They exceeded my expectations for customer service – far better than what I had at any of the manufacturer dealerships. My sales rep at Shift Motors, Simeon, was so transparent in the process that I felt very comfortable going with the used vehicle.

If you want to try a variety of electric vehicles, I would strongly recommend heading to Shift Motors in Oakville. Since they are an EV only dealership, and you can try all of the makes/models in one location.

I have no relationship with Shift Motors, I’m sharing this because it was an exceptionally great experience and I feel good customer service and honest sales should be rewarded.

What electric vehicles are out there? What did you try? What would you recommend?

As you might imagine, I researched all of them and I tried a lot of them. I wanted at least 500km of range, which led me to try the vehicles below.

Prices below are for the extended range battery models as of August 2024, in Canadian dollars, with Ontario pricing, and do not include dealer discounts, tax, or Federal ($5,000) or Provincial rebates:

  • Volkswagen id.4 Pro – $55,728: I loved it. It’s the same size as a Tiguan, with a luxury quality interior. The screen/UI setup was the best of any EV I tried. The drive was fun and sporty. It had the quietest cabin inside. It gets over 500km of range. The only knock on it is the lack of Tesla Supercharger integration – VW has promised it in 2025? Maybe? If you mostly drive locally and can charge at home, with occasional road trips, this is the one I would buy.
